easy.title: Reading the address
easy.body: The browser separates the name you typed into useful pieces. It recognizes where you want to go before sending anything.

real.title: URL parsing
real.body: The address is parsed into a scheme, hostname, port, path, query, and fragment. Invalid host characters are converted with IDNA/Punycode before name resolution.
real.interviewLine: The browser first parses and normalizes the URL into the fields needed by the network stack.

easy.title: A shortcut check
easy.body: The browser checks whether it already knows the answer. A fresh saved copy can skip much of the trip.

real.title: Cache hierarchy
real.body: The browser checks memory and disk caches, then relies on OS-level caches for DNS and network state. A valid cached response may be reused or revalidated.
real.interviewLine: Caches can satisfy or shorten the request before a new network connection is opened.

easy.title: Ask the resolver
easy.body: DNS is the internet’s phonebook. Your resolver takes the name google.com and starts looking for its number.

real.title: Recursive resolver
real.body: The stub resolver asks its configured recursive resolver for google.com. The resolver answers from cache or performs iterative queries on the client’s behalf.
real.interviewLine: The client asks a recursive resolver, which either serves a cached record or walks the DNS hierarchy.

easy.title: Start at the root
easy.body: The first guide does not know Google’s address, but it knows where .com lives. It points the question onward.

real.title: Root nameserver referral
real.body: A root nameserver returns a referral to the .com TLD nameservers. This is an iterative referral, not the final A or AAAA record.
real.interviewLine: The root server delegates the lookup to the appropriate top-level-domain nameservers.

easy.title: Find .com
easy.body: The .com guide knows which directory holds Google’s entry. One more handoff gets us close.

real.title: TLD referral
real.body: A .com TLD nameserver returns the authoritative nameserver set for google.com, typically with glue when needed to avoid another circular lookup.
real.interviewLine: The TLD server points the resolver to the domain’s authoritative nameservers.

easy.title: The final answer
easy.body: Google’s own directory returns an IP address. The glowing query now carries the number back to your browser.

real.title: Authoritative answer
real.body: The authoritative server returns an A or AAAA answer with a TTL. The resolver caches the result and sends it to the client; the displayed 142.250.x.x is illustrative.
real.interviewLine: The authoritative answer supplies the address and TTL that downstream caches may reuse.

easy.title: Can we talk?
easy.body: Your computer sends a hello across the gap. It asks the server to open a reliable connection.

real.title: SYN
real.body: The client sends a TCP segment with SYN set and an initial sequence number to the server’s destination port.
real.interviewLine: SYN proposes a connection and establishes the client’s initial sequence space.

easy.title: I hear you
easy.body: The server answers that it is ready and heard the hello. Two pieces of the bridge lock together.

real.title: SYN-ACK
real.body: The server acknowledges the client sequence number and sends its own SYN with a server initial sequence number.
real.interviewLine: SYN-ACK proves the server received the client’s SYN and contributes its own sequence number.

easy.title: Connection ready
easy.body: Your computer confirms the reply. The final bridge piece clicks in and data can cross.

real.title: ACK
real.body: The client acknowledges the server’s sequence number. Both sides now agree on connection state and can exchange ordered bytes.
real.interviewLine: The final ACK confirms both directions and completes the TCP connection.

easy.title: Check the identity
easy.body: The site shows a hard-to-forge identity card. Your browser checks that it belongs to Google and was signed by someone it trusts.

real.title: Certificate chain
real.body: The server certificate binds a public key to the hostname. The browser verifies signatures up to a trusted root, hostname coverage, validity, and revocation signals.
real.interviewLine: Certificate validation authenticates the server before application data is trusted.

easy.title: Create secret keys
easy.body: Both sides mix private ingredients into matching secret keys. The secret itself never travels across the network.

real.title: Ephemeral key agreement
real.body: Modern TLS negotiates parameters and uses ephemeral key agreement to derive symmetric traffic keys. TLS 1.3 normally completes a full handshake in one round trip.
real.interviewLine: TLS derives fast symmetric session keys after authenticating the server.

easy.title: Wrap the packet
easy.body: The packet gains glowing armor. From here on, anyone watching the road sees scrambled data instead of your request.

real.title: Encrypted records
real.body: HTTP headers and bodies are carried inside authenticated TLS records. Encryption provides confidentiality while authentication detects tampering.
real.interviewLine: After the handshake, HTTP travels inside authenticated, encrypted TLS records.

kicker: ONE ADDRESS, A GLOBAL FRONT DOOR

easy.title: A nearby entrance
easy.body: The same address is advertised from many places. The network steers your packet toward a nearby Google edge.

real.title: Anycast routing
real.body: Multiple edge sites can advertise the same prefix with BGP. Network routing selects a reachable path; “nearest” means routing-topology proximity, not physical distance.
real.interviewLine: Anycast lets one service address lead users toward a suitable nearby edge site.

easy.title: Sort the traffic
easy.body: A load balancer is a traffic conductor. It sends each request to a healthy machine with room to help.

real.title: Edge load balancing
real.body: The edge may terminate transport and TLS, apply policy, and route the HTTP request across healthy backends using locality, capacity, and service metadata.
real.interviewLine: The edge terminates and routes traffic so individual backends are hidden behind one service.

easy.title: Millions of journeys
easy.body: Your packet joins a river of requests. Shared infrastructure keeps every tiny journey moving without collisions.

real.title: Multiplexed traffic
real.body: Persistent connections and multiplexing let many request streams share infrastructure efficiently. HTTP/2 multiplexes over TCP; HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC over UDP.
real.interviewLine: Modern transports multiplex many logical request streams across fewer long-lived connections.

easy.title: Read the request
easy.body: A server opens the packet and sees what page you asked for. It checks the request before choosing an answer.

real.title: HTTP request parsing
real.body: The front end parses the method, path, headers, cookies, and request body, then applies routing, authentication, policy, and observability.
real.interviewLine: The server parses HTTP and routes the request into the application pipeline.

easy.title: Assemble the response
easy.body: Fast caches provide familiar pieces; other parts are computed. The server packs the page instructions for the trip back.

real.title: Cache or compute
real.body: The application may satisfy the request from an edge or service cache, call backend services, or query storage before serializing an HTTP response.
real.interviewLine: Request handling is usually a cache-first pipeline before deeper service or storage work.

easy.title: Turn code into pixels
easy.body: Back in the browser, page instructions become a tree of visible pieces. The browser sizes, paints, and layers them into the page you see.

real.title: DOM to pixels
real.body: The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, builds a render tree, performs layout, paints layers, and composites them—while fetching discovered subresources.
real.interviewLine: Rendering proceeds through DOM/CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, and compositing.
